title: Intermediate Python
summary: From scripts to real programs: functions used properly, the right data structure for each job, errors handled, your own classes, tests that prove the code works, and a command line. It ends with a library manager built from classes, with tests and a command line.
prereq: PY1 · Python Foundations at Intermediate: functions, lists and dictionaries, loops, files and try/except.
outcomes: Write functions with defaults, named and any number of arguments, and pass functions around with key= and lambda.
Pick the right structure: tuples, sets, dictionaries and comprehensions, and the collections module.
Handle errors on purpose: catch, raise and define your own exceptions.
Design classes with methods, properties and inheritance, and use dataclasses.
Prove code works with tests, written first when it helps.
Build a command-line program that saves its data as JSON: the library manager.

levels.name: Intermediate
levels.who: Anyone who finished PY1 and wants to write real programs; what PY3 and most streams expect.
levels.outcome: Write clean functions, classes and tests, and build the library manager with a command line.

levels.name: Master
levels.who: Future developers who want the depth behind the tools: closures, decorators, generators and design.
levels.outcome: Use closures, decorators, generators and dunder methods, and design the library manager to grow.

levelNote: PY2 starts at Intermediate, where PY1 stops.

upcoming.title: Inheritance and design
upcoming.summary: Subclasses and super(), composition, dunder methods for comparing and sorting, and when not to use a class.

upcoming.title: Tests, JSON and the command line
upcoming.summary: assert and pytest-style tests, test-first, JSON files, modules and a command line with argparse: the library manager’s shape.

project.title: A library manager with classes, tests and a command line
project.brief: Books, members and loans as classes, saved to a JSON file, driven from a command line, with tests that prove the rules (no lending a book that is out, fines on late returns). A checklist per level, hidden tests and three “explain your code” questions.

modules.title: Functions, properly

lessons.title: Default and named arguments
lessons.summary: A parameter can have a default value, used when the call leaves it out: def fine(days, rate=2). A call can name its values, fine(days=5, rate=3), so the order no longer matters and the call says what each number means. Values by position come first, named ones after; in a def, parameters with defaults come after the ones without.

lessons.title: Class methods and static methods
lessons.summary: @classmethod gets the class itself as cls instead of an object, which makes it the place for other ways to build one: Book.from_line("Godan; Premchand; 1936"). Using cls(…) rather than Book(…) means subclasses get objects of their own type. @staticmethod gets neither: it is a plain function that lives in the class because it belongs with it, like Book.valid_code("FIC-0042").
